title: NY State Senate · District 27
area: Lower Manhattan (East Village, Gramercy, Lower East Side, Chinatown, Financial District, Battery Park City) and northwest Brooklyn (Brooklyn Heights, DUMBO, Williamsburg, Greenpoint).

context.text: Open seat: incumbent Brian Kavanagh (D) did not file for re-election. Assemblymember Grace Lee defeated former Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou 62.5%-37.3% in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary.

Niou separately won the Working Families Party primary, but Ballotpedia lists her as a withdrawn/disqualified candidate for the general election; she does not appear on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot, which is a two-candidate race between Lee and Jason Murillo.

candidates.name: Grace Lee
candidates.currentRole: New York State Assemblymember, District 65 (since 2023); not seeking re-election to the Assembly

summary.text: Grace Lee is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for the open NY Senate District 27 seat. She is the current Assemblymember for District 65 (Lower Manhattan), first elected in 2022, and the first Korean American woman elected to the New York State Legislature. She chairs the Assembly's Asian Pacific American Task Force and is not seeking re-election to her Assembly seat.

background.text: Earned a B.A. in economics and philosophy from Columbia University (2002) and an M.B.A. in finance and entrepreneurship from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business (2010).
Co-founded Children First, a coalition focused on mercury brownfield cleanup, and co-founded Nine Naturals, a beauty products company, before running for office.
First elected to the NY State Assembly in 2022, succeeding Yuh-Line Niou in District 65; re-elected in 2024 with 99.1% of the vote.

Serves on the Assembly's Banks, Children and Families, Consumer Affairs and Protection, Environmental Conservation, and Housing committees (2025-2026), and chairs the Asian Pacific American Task Force.

priorities.text: Housing affordability: protect rent-stabilized tenants and expand emergency rental assistance, having secured nearly $400 million through ERAP for NYCHA and Section 8 residents.
Universal childcare and expanded pre-K, building on $2 billion in statewide childcare investments she says she helped secure ($350 million for NYC).
Limit state and local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement (ICE), including barring ICE from schools, hospitals, and places of worship.
Raise taxes on the highest earners and close corporate tax loopholes, including support for a pied-a-terre tax on second homes valued at $5 million or more.
Expand access to healthcare, including co-sponsoring the New York Health Act to create a universal single-payer system and lowering prescription drug costs.

positions.summary: Campaign platform supports Good Cause Eviction protections against unreasonable rent increases and retaliatory evictions, and funding legal services for tenants facing harassment.

Platform calls for ending most state and local cooperation with ICE, banning contracts between local jails and ICE, and keeping ICE out of schools, hospitals, and places of worship; co-sponsors the New York for All Act.
Supports higher income-tax rates on the highest earners, a wealth tax on the richest households, closing corporate tax loopholes, and a surcharge on second homes valued at $5 million or more.
Co-sponsors the New York Health Act to establish a universal single-payer healthcare system and supports a state-funded essential plan for low- and moderate-income New Yorkers.
Platform states she is fighting for statewide universal childcare access, citing past work securing billions in statewide childcare investment.
Platform supports a statewide clean fuel standard for transportation, expanding NYPA's renewable-power role, and requiring corporate emissions transparency.

Platform supports protecting the privacy of abortion providers and patients, backed the 2024 reproductive-freedom ballot measure, and says she helped secure $25 million for the state's Abortion Access Program.
Platform supports Manhattan congestion pricing while seeking an exemption for Lower and Midtown Manhattan residents earning under $60,000.

record.text: Sponsored and helped pass the Hate Crimes Modernization Act, described by her office as the first update to New York's hate crimes statute in more than two decades.
Led the legislative effort making New York the first state to designate Lunar New Year as a statewide school holiday.
Introduced the STOP Act, aimed at increasing institutional accountability following the conduct findings against former Governor Andrew Cuomo.
Says she secured nearly $400 million in Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) funding for NYCHA and Section 8 households in her first year in office (2023).

Chairs the Assembly's Asian Pacific American Task Force and serves on the Banks, Children and Families, Consumer Affairs and Protection, Environmental Conservation, and Housing committees in the 2025-2026 session.

summary.text: Jason Murillo is the Republican and Conservative Party nominee for the open NY Senate District 27 seat. An attorney also known by the nickname "DJ Loud Mouth," he has not previously held elected office and unsuccessfully sought the Republican nomination for a February 2026 special election to NY Assembly District 74, for which he did not ultimately appear on the ballot.

background.text: Born in New York, NY; graduated from Seward Park High School.

Works as a politician/attorney and has been active in Manhattan and citywide Republican and Conservative Party organizations, including the Manhattan Republican Party and Manhattan Conservative County Committee.

Sought the Republican nomination for the February 3, 2026 special election in NY Assembly District 74, which was ultimately won by Keith Powers (D) over Joseph Foley (R/C); Murillo did not appear on that special-election ballot.

researchNotes: No campaign website or detailed policy statements were found for Jason Murillo; Ballotpedia notes he has not completed its Candidate Connection survey and has no prior officeholding record, so his entry is limited to biographical facts from Ballotpedia. Per Ballotpedia, Yuh-Line Niou won the June 2026 Working Families Party primary for this seat but is listed as withdrawn/not appearing on the November 3 general-election ballot, superseding the July 2026 snapshot data that showed her as a WFP-line general-election candidate; she is therefore not included as a candidate in this file.
